30-8.title: Screen a teenager for depression with a proper tool and a trained adult, not a school assembly
30-8.inPlainWords: A school mental-health survey is not a diagnosis. If a teenager has two weeks of low mood, lost interest, sleep or appetite change, or thoughts of self-harm, use a validated questionnaire such as the PHQ-A and have a trained counsellor or doctor interpret it. The District Mental Health Programme and Tele-MANAS on 14416 can help. Do not rely on a single score or a teacher's impression.
30-8.benefit: The National Mental Health Programme and the District Mental Health Programme place mental-health services in district hospitals; school counsellors and the Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram adolescent health clinics are the local route. A validated tool is a screening aid, not a diagnosis. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 protects the rights of a person with a mental illness and requires informed consent. A school should have a referral protocol, not a public ranking.
30-8.cost: A government consultation is free or low cost. Tele-MANAS on 14416 is free.
30-8.caveats: A screening result should stay confidential. A positive screen needs a clinical assessment, not a label. If there is a risk of suicide, do not leave the teenager alone; call 14416 or 112.
30-8.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Mental Health Programme. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Tele-MANAS. <https://telemanas.mohfw.gov.in/>; Mental Healthcare Act, 2017. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

30-15.title: If a child says they are attracted to the same sex, listen and protect them — do not send them for 'conversion'
30-15.inPlainWords: In India, consensual same-sex relations between adults are not a crime after the Supreme Court's judgment in Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India (2018). A parent's rejection, a forced 'conversion' or a threat to throw the child out increases the risk of depression and suicide. Listen, keep the child safe, and if you need help, call Tele-MANAS on 14416 or a counsellor who does not promise to change orientation.
30-15.benefit: The Supreme Court read down section 377 of the Indian Penal Code in 2018, so consensual same-sex conduct between adults is not an offence. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 prohibits discrimination in mental-health care and requires informed consent. 'Conversion therapy' is not a recognised treatment and is opposed by the Indian Psychiatric Society. A family that rejects a child increases the risk of homelessness and self-harm.
30-15.cost: No cost to listen. A counsellor costs money; Tele-MANAS is free.
30-15.caveats: A minor may still face bullying at school and a hostile relative. Do not out the child to others without consent. If the child is in danger at home, contact Childline on 1098 or the police.
30-15.sources: Supreme Court of India, Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India (2018). <https://www.sci.gov.in/>; Mental Healthcare Act, 2017. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Tele-MANAS. <https://telemanas.mohfw.gov.in/>; Indian Psychiatric Society. <https://indianpsychiatricsociety.org/>

30-2.caveats: Scoliosis is a good example because it has randomized trials, a clear treatment window, and it turns up in school screening. Strabismus, amblyopia, dental caries and some elective cardiac surgery behave the same way: later treatment gives a worse result or costs more. Missing some school is not a reason to delay treatment, but a long absence has to be arranged with the school in advance, because India has no national rule that keeps a child's seat open for a year (item 11). Ask the orthopaedic surgeon when the brace must start and how often it will be reviewed, and get that in writing for the school.

30-3.title: Bullying is not a personality problem: report it in writing the same day, and escalate if the school does not act
30-3.cost: No cost. Put the complaint in writing, keep a copy, and ask for a written reply. A police complaint is free; dial 112 in an emergency. The hard part is resisting the pressure to keep it quiet.
30-3.inPlainWords: Children who are bullied are about 2.2 times more likely to have suicidal thoughts and about 2.6 times more likely to attempt suicide. India has no single national anti-bullying statute, so the route is layered: the school's own anti-bullying or grievance committee, which boards and state education departments require; section 17 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, which bars physical punishment and mental harassment in school; and the criminal law, because assault, threats and theft are offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Reporting the same day and demanding a written response matters more than asking the teacher to have a word.
30-3.benefit: The conclusion rests on 34 studies of 284,375 children and adolescents. Peer bullying is linked to suicidal thoughts with an OR of 2.23 (95% CI 2.10-2.37), and nine further studies with 70,102 participants link it to suicide attempts with an OR of 2.55 (1.95-3.34). The association held across sex, age and study quality, and cyberbullying was linked more strongly to suicidal thoughts than physical bullying. On the Indian side, section 17 of the RTE Act, 2009 prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment and makes a breach a disciplinary matter; a school run without a grievance mechanism can be taken up with the district education officer; and the State Commission for Protection of Child Rights, set up under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, can take up a school that ignores a written complaint. Assault, criminal intimidation and mischief are offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and an FIR can be filed at any police station.
30-3.caveats: Unexplained injuries, a sudden refusal to go to school or repeated loss of belongings deserve a written complaint with dates. This evidence is observational, so it shows a strong association rather than proof that bullying alone causes suicide. Distinguish bullying from ordinary rough play, and ask the school which committee handles it and on what timeline. Keep copies of every letter. Grade B because the association is strong but the studies are observational.
30-3.sources: van Geel M, Vedder P, Tanilon J (2014). Relationship between peer victimization, cyberbullying, and suicide in children and adolescents: a meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics, 168(5), 435-442. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2013.4143>; Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. <https://www.education.gov.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Commission for Protection of Child Rights. <https://ncpcr.gov.in/>

30-4.title: Get children outdoors every day: extra daylight is the best-evidenced way to delay myopia, and the two-hour target is a convention rather than a rule
30-4.cost: No cost. It needs school time and an adult who will take the child out after school. The trial added 40 minutes to the school day, so an hour outdoors is already most of the effect.
30-4.inPlainWords: A randomized trial in 12 primary schools in Guangzhou gave first-grade children an extra 40 minutes of outdoor activity each school day. After three years the rate of new myopia was 30.4% in those schools against 39.5% in the control schools, a difference of 9.1 percentage points. The two-hour-a-day figure that is often quoted is a convention from myopia policy in East Asia, not an Indian or World Health Organization rule; what the trial supports is more daylight, and it added only 40 minutes. Cloudy days and outdoor recess still count.
30-4.benefit: First-grade children in the 12 schools were randomized to the intervention or the control group (952 and 951 children, mean age 6.6 years). The intervention added a 40-minute outdoor class each day and encouraged parents to take the child outdoors after school. Over three years the rate of new myopia was 30.4% in the intervention group (259 of 853 eligible) against 39.5% in the control group (287 of 726), a difference of -9.1 percentage points (95% CI -14.1 to -4.1, P<0.001). The mean increase in refractive error was -1.42 D in the intervention group against -1.59 D in the control group, a difference of 0.17 D (P=0.04), so progression was slightly slower. There was no significant difference in axial length (P=0.07). Daylight is not the only intervention with trial evidence: atropine eye drops and defocus spectacle lenses have randomized trials behind them too, but they need a doctor, and daylight is the cheapest.
30-4.caveats: The trial ran three years in children who started at age 6, and a 9.1-point difference means some children are protected, not that any child is guaranteed protection. The intervention was school time plus encouragement at home, so a family that manages an hour outdoors has captured much of it. Reading distance, the 20-20-20 break and screen limits are sensible but rest on weaker evidence than daylight (items 5 and 9). Grade B because the trial is strong but the effect is partial and measured over three years only.
30-4.sources: He M, Xiang F, Zeng Y, et al. (2015). Effect of time spent outdoors at school on the development of myopia among children: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA, 314(11), 1142-1148. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.10803>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>

30-5.title: Screens: keep them away from babies and toddlers, and cap recreational use for older children. India sets no age-banded rule, so this is a family decision
30-5.cost: No cost. The effort is in holding the line when a screen is the easiest way to keep a child quiet, and in arranging something else to do.
30-5.inPlainWords: India has no national rule that sets screen hours by age. The World Health Organization's guidance for children under five says sedentary screen time is not recommended for a child under two, and that for two- to four-year-olds it should be no more than an hour a day, with less being better. For school-age children the evidence is weaker: heavy screen use is associated with slightly higher odds of myopia, and with poorer language development when it displaces talk with caregivers. The strongest single habit remains outdoor daylight (item 4).
30-5.benefit: A systematic review covered 33 studies with participants from 3 months to 33 years; only 11 entered the pooled analysis. For smartphones and tablets alone the odds ratio for myopia was 1.26 (95% CI 1.00-1.60, I2 = 77%), and including computers raised it to 1.77 (1.28-2.45, I2 = 87%). The authors concluded only that a link may exist, because none of the 33 studies measured screen time reliably. A separate meta-analysis of 42 studies found a small negative association between screen use and language development (r = -0.14). In India the limit is set by the family and the school rather than by law; the WHO guidance for the under-fives is the only official age-banded figure available.
30-5.caveats: Grade B because the guidance is policy plus observational evidence, not a trial of screen limits. Reading on a screen and video-calling a grandparent are not the same as an hour of short videos. If a preschool child is squinting, rubbing the eyes or holding a book very close, get an eye examination at a district hospital rather than adjusting the screen (item 12). The under-five WHO figure does not answer the question for a 10-year-old, and this book will not invent one.
30-5.sources: Foreman J, Salim AT, Praveen A, et al. (2021). Association between digital smart device use and myopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Digital Health, 3(12), e806-e818. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2589-7500(21)00135-7>; Madigan S, McArthur BA, Anhorn C, Eirich R, Christakis DA (2020). Associations between screen use and child language skills: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics, 174(7), 665-675. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2020.0327>; World Health Organization (2019). Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age. <https://www.who.int/>

30-6.cost: No cost. There is nothing specific to do here; the actions are in items 4 and 5 (daylight and screen limits) and item 12 (follow-up).
30-6.inPlainWords: Myopia does not go away on its own and the prescription does not fall. It is more than a pair of glasses. Compared with someone without myopia, a person with mild myopia has roughly 10 to 15 times the odds of myopic macular degeneration, and at a prescription of -6.00 D or stronger the odds rise by several hundred times. Retinal detachment is about three times more likely in mild myopia and about 13 times more likely in high myopia. The earlier a child becomes myopic and the faster it progresses, the larger the lifetime risk.
30-6.benefit: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled studies published to June 2019 into three groups: mild (-0.5 to -3.00 D), moderate (-3.00 to -6.00 D) and high (-6.00 D or stronger). Against people without myopia, the odds ratios for myopic macular degeneration were 13.57 (95% CI 6.18-29.79) for mild, 72.74 (33.18-159.48) for moderate and 845.08 (230.05-3104.34) for high myopia. For retinal detachment they were 3.15 (1.92-5.17), 8.74 (7.28-10.50) and 12.62 (6.65-23.94). For posterior subcapsular cataract they were 1.56 (1.32-1.84), 2.55 (1.98-3.28) and 4.55 (2.66-7.75). For open-angle glaucoma the odds ratio was 1.59 (1.33-1.91) for mild myopia and 2.92 (1.89-4.52) for moderate and high myopia combined. Among people over 60 the odds ratios for visual impairment were 1.71 (1.07-2.74), 5.54 (3.12-9.85) and 87.63 (34.50-222.58). High myopia is the group at -6.00 D or stronger, and it carries higher rates of cataract, open-angle glaucoma, myopic macular degeneration and retinal detachment. Myopia can be prevented or slowed but not reversed.

30-7.title: Look closely at the school health screening result and follow up any abnormality in the same year
30-7.cost: Free. Screening under the National Child Health Programme and the treatment it leads to at a government facility are free. Private tests and private hospitals are extra.
30-7.inPlainWords: Under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram, part of the National Child Health Programme, children from birth to 18 are screened for four groups of problems: defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays, across 32 common conditions. Screening happens at delivery points, at anganwadis and at government schools, and a child who screens positive is referred on, including to a District Early Intervention Centre, with free treatment up to tertiary surgery. Private and aided schools are not automatically covered, so ask what your school actually runs. Overweight, poor vision, spinal curvature and dental cavities are the findings parents most often file away.
30-7.benefit: The programme screens at the delivery point, at the anganwadi and at government schools, and it lets States empanel private hospitals for conditions such as cardiac defects and congenital problems so that the family does not pay. The referral chain runs from the screening point to the district hospital or the District Early Intervention Centre and, for a disability, to the disability certificate route. A private school usually runs its own annual check, which is not the same instrument and does not refer into the free system. The report to look at is the one with the referral slip attached, not the height and weight line.
30-7.caveats: Screening is not a diagnosis: a flagged vision or hearing result needs a proper examination (item 12). The programme covers anganwadi and government-school children, and private-school children may only be reached if a State has extended it, so confirm locally. Keep the card and the referral slip, because the district hospital will ask for them. Grade B because the pathway is administrative and the evidence for annual screening itself is not from randomized trials.
30-7.sources: National Health Mission, Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram. <https://nhm.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Ministry of Education. <https://www.education.gov.in/>

30-9.title: Nothing cures myopia: treat a cure claim as a misleading advertisement, which is an offence under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
30-9.cost: No cost to check. If you have already paid, a complaint to the consumer commission costs a nominal fee and can be filed online.
30-9.inPlainWords: No product cures myopia, and no lens, exercise, massage or supplement reverses a refractive error. Claims that a product restores vision, reduces the prescription or repairs the eye are misleading, and in India a misleading advertisement is an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The Central Consumer Protection Authority can order the advertisement withdrawn and penalise the advertiser, a district consumer commission can order a refund and compensation, and the Advertising Standards Council of India screens complaints about health claims. If a seller promises a cure, stop comparing products.
30-9.benefit: The consumer route is the Indian one. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines a misleading advertisement, treats it as an unfair trade practice, and gives the Central Consumer Protection Authority power to investigate, order discontinuation and impose a penalty; a consumer commission can award a refund and compensation. The Advertising Standards Council of India's code covers misleading health claims and accepts complaints from consumers. Contact lenses and some optical devices are regulated as medical devices by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, so a seller needs the licence that goes with that. None of this makes a cure exist: the measures with evidence are daylight (item 4), correct glasses and review (item 12), and in some children atropine or defocus lenses prescribed by an ophthalmologist.
30-9.caveats: Grade B because the basis is a regulatory position and the absence of evidence, not a trial of a particular product. Preventable and controllable but not reversible is the accurate summary. Blue-light-blocking lenses are covered in chapter 6. If a child's prescription is climbing quickly, see an ophthalmologist rather than buying a device.
30-9.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Central Consumer Protection Authority. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Advertising Standards Council of India. <https://www.ascionline.in/>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/>

30-10.title: India has no national rule on sleep hours, homework caps or school start times: ask the school for its written policy and protect sleep at home
30-10.cost: No cost. The work is one written request to the school and a bedtime you can actually keep.
30-10.inPlainWords: India has no statute that fixes how many hours a school-age child must sleep, how much homework may be set, when school starts or whether results may be ranked. What exists is weaker: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 bars physical punishment and mental harassment and stops a school expelling a child before the end of elementary education; boards and state education departments issue circulars from time to time; and the school's prospectus or diary usually states its own homework and reporting practice. The World Health Organization recommends at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for children aged 5 to 17, and that figure is worth quoting to a school.
30-10.benefit: Rules differ by State, board and school, and a private school's obligations come mainly from its affiliation bye-laws and its own published policy, so there is no single document to quote at a principal. Use three levers: a written request for the school's homework, assessment and reporting policy; the school's grievance committee, which the RTE framework and board affiliation rules require; and the district education officer, who can act where a school breaches the RTE Act's prohibition on harassment. On sleep and activity the family has more control than the school: a fixed bedtime, no screen in the bedroom and an hour outdoors are the parts you can change this week (items 4 and 5).
30-10.caveats: Grade B because the rules vary by State, board and school, and this book will not quote a national number that does not exist. Publishing marks and ranks is common in Indian schools and is not by itself illegal, though a school should follow its own stated policy. If a child is persistently short of sleep, the usual cause is bedtime and commute, not a rule to enforce. The WHO figure is a recommendation, not Indian law.
30-10.sources: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. <https://www.education.gov.in/>; Ministry of Education. <https://www.education.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>

30-11.title: There is no national entitlement to a year's leave with the seat kept: what the RTE Act does say, and what to ask the school in writing
30-11.cost: No fee. Put the request in writing and keep a copy. The hard part is accepting that the child needs the break and then arranging the return.
30-11.inPlainWords: India has no equivalent of a statutory one-year leave of absence with the enrolment retained. A school records attendance, and a long absence is treated as a gap in schooling rather than as protected leave. What the law does give you: a child who is out of school must be admitted to a class appropriate to his or her age, a school cannot expel a child before the end of elementary education, and the State must provide a neighbourhood school. For a child over 14, or in a private school, everything depends on the school's own rules and on the board's examination rules.
30-11.benefit: Read the provisions together. Section 3 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 gives every child aged 6 to 14 a right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school. Section 4 requires a child who has not been admitted, or who has dropped out, to be admitted to a class appropriate to his or her age, with special training where needed. Section 16 bars expulsion and, since the 2019 amendment, allows a State that has notified it to hold a child back in classes 5 and 8 after a re-examination. None of these creates a right to keep a seat empty for a year, and a private unaided school is bound by its own admission rules on top of the Act.
30-11.caveats: Ask three questions in writing before the break: what document the school needs, whether the child's name stays on the rolls, and whether the child returns to the same class or is placed by age. A long absence for medical treatment should be documented with hospital papers. If the school refuses to take the child back, section 4 is the provision to quote and the district education officer is the route. Grade B because the clinical advice is standard but the administrative answer differs by State and board.
30-11.sources: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. <https://www.education.gov.in/>; Ministry of Education. <https://www.education.gov.in/>

30-12.title: If screening flags poor vision, get a proper eye examination with drops that relax the focusing muscle, and keep the review the ophthalmologist sets
30-12.cost: An eye examination at a government hospital is free or nominal; glasses, a private clinic and contact lenses cost extra. The drops blur near vision for a few hours, so plan a half day.
30-12.inPlainWords: A school or anganwadi screening only flags a possible problem. The diagnosis is made by an eye doctor using cycloplegic refraction: drops relax the focusing muscle so the true refractive error can be measured, which matters most in young children whose focusing can hide longsightedness. A computerised reading at an optical shop is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Do not withhold glasses because someone says they weaken the eyes; that is not how myopia works.
30-12.benefit: Cycloplegic refraction is the standard diagnostic step in children, and the drops are safe for healthy eyes; light sensitivity and blurred near vision are temporary. If myopia is confirmed, corrected glasses are the first step and they do not make the eyes worse. India has no national guideline that fixes review intervals, so the interval is a clinical decision: an ophthalmologist will usually want a young child back sooner than a teenager, and sooner again if the prescription is changing fast or the child has a squint, a lazy eye or a strong family history. High myopia carries a lifetime risk of retinal detachment, myopic macular degeneration and glaucoma (item 6), so review is not only about a new pair of glasses. District hospitals and medical college ophthalmology departments run refraction services, and a screening referral reaches them.
30-12.caveats: Grade B because the practice is standard but no Indian document fixes intervals, and this book will not invent one. The drops cause light sensitivity and blurred near vision for some hours, so a child should not cycle home alone afterwards. A prescription from an optical shop without a doctor's examination is not a diagnosis for a child. Bring the screening card to the appointment.
30-12.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Mission, Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram. <https://nhm.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>

30-13.cost: A sealant at a government dental hospital or a school dental camp is free or nominal; a private dentist charges per tooth, so ask before the appointment. No anaesthetic and no drilling, and the tooth takes a few minutes.
30-13.caveats: The first permanent molars, which are never replaced, appear around age 6, and the second molars near age 12. A sealant goes on as soon as the molar erupts and before decay starts; once a cavity has formed the sealant cannot be used and a filling is needed. No Indian national document with coverage criteria or age limits could be identified, so those details are omitted. Dental caries remains one of the findings that school screening is meant to catch (item 7).

30-14.title: If a child plays a lot of games, first check what it is crowding out, such as sleep, homework and outdoor time, rather than counting hours
30-14.cost: No cost. The effort is in agreeing a house rule that everyone follows, including the adults.
30-14.inPlainWords: Only about two or three children in a hundred meet the criteria for gaming disorder; surveys with low thresholds and teenage-only samples report much higher figures. Real play data shows almost no link between hours played and how happy a player feels. India has no legal curfew on the hours a minor may play, so the limit is yours to set. What predicts trouble is displacement: late nights, skipped homework and no time outdoors.
30-14.benefit: One meta-analysis combined 53 studies from 17 countries with 226,247 participants. The overall prevalence of gaming disorder was 3.05% (95% CI 2.38-3.91), and with stricter sampling criteria it fell to 1.96%. Differences between studies come largely from the questionnaire used, and small samples with low thresholds inflate the rate. Another study compared actual gameplay data from 38,935 players over six weeks with self-reported happiness and found virtually no evidence that playing time affects wellbeing. In India the practical safeguards are the family rule, the platform's parental controls, and the consumer route if a child runs up in-app purchases, because the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers unfair trade practices and a payment made by a minor can be disputed with the platform and the bank.
30-14.caveats: Grade B because prevalence depends on the questionnaire and the wellbeing study ran six weeks. The main harm of heavy gaming is displacement of sleep and outdoor activity (items 4 and 10). If school performance, sleep and family relationships all deteriorate despite changes, see a child psychiatrist or paediatric psychologist. Do not use a residential detox centre (item 18).
30-14.sources: Stevens MW, Dorstyn D, Delfabbro PH, King DL (2021). Global prevalence of gaming disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry, 55(6), 553-568. <https://doi.org/10.1177/0004867420962851>; Vuorre M, Johannes N, Magnusson K, Przybylski AK (2022). Time spent playing video games is unlikely to impact well-being. Royal Society Open Science, 9(7), 220411. <https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220411>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>

30-17.cost: A multi-week course is not free in India. Some hospitals, anganwadi parenting sessions and school programmes run at no charge; a private course costs money, so ask the price before enrolling.
30-17.inPlainWords: Parenting programmes that teach specific techniques reduce children's hitting and rule-breaking in randomized trials, and parents' mood improves. Parents also hit and yell less, most strongly right after the course, still measurably one to two years later but much smaller. India has few public multi-week courses, so look for a course run by a hospital child-guidance unit, a recognised programme, or an anganwadi parenting session rather than a one-off lecture.
30-17.benefit: Cochrane pooled 13 trials, 10 randomized, with 1,078 parents of children aged 3 to 12 who had behaviour problems. After training, children's behaviour problems decreased: parent report SMD -0.53 (95% CI -0.72 to -0.34), independent raters -0.44 (-0.77 to -0.11). SMD is the same scale as d, where 0.5 is a medium effect. Parent mental health improved by -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20). Harsh parenting decreased: parent report -0.77 (-0.96 to -0.59), independent -0.42 (-0.67 to -0.16). The authors call these short-term effects. A second meta-analysis screened 346 randomized trials; 60 measured hitting or yelling across 22 countries. Hitting and yelling fell immediately after the course, d = -0.46 (-0.59 to -0.33), then -0.24 (-0.37 to -0.11) at 1 to 6 months and -0.18 (-0.34 to -0.02) at 7 to 24 months, fading over time. Most of the data are parent-reported. A rural kindergarten trial with 191 caregivers compared self-paced online lessons plus two group discussions with a book alone: after two weeks self-reported abusive behaviour was about 33% lower (IRR 0.67), and at three months children's behaviour problems were lower (d = -0.40).
30-17.caveats: Grade A from Cochrane and pooled randomized trials. The courses that worked shared features: an instructor teaches concrete skills (play, praise, rewards, discipline), parents practise and get homework. Programmes that only handed out material or only held a discussion were excluded, so the evidence does not cover a one-off lecture. Content of local programmes varies and may not match this model, so look for a multi-week course with practice. Names often include Triple P, Incredible Years and Parent-Child Interaction Therapy. This book does not endorse a provider or a paid product. The reduction in hitting fades after one to two years, so keep practising after the course ends. If the child already has severe emotional problems, see a child psychiatrist (item 8).

30-18.title: Never send a child to an enclosed internet-addiction or discipline camp: confinement is unlawful in India and there is no evidence it works
30-18.cost: No fee, and it saves what such a centre charges. The hard part is refusing to outsource discipline when things are at breaking point.
30-18.inPlainWords: A centre that locks a child in, restrains them, withholds food or beats them is committing offences under Indian law, whatever the brochure says. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 requires an institution that houses children to be registered as a child care institution and punishes cruelty to a child; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers wrongful confinement, hurt and criminal intimidation; the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 covers sexual abuse and makes reporting mandatory; and the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 governs admission and treatment for mental illness. No good evidence shows that confinement treats heavy gaming.
30-18.benefit: The legal route is the practical route. A child care institution must be registered under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, and running an unregistered one is an offence; the Act also punishes assault, abandonment and wilful neglect of a child by the person in charge. Wrongful confinement and hurt are offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 sets the conditions for admitting and treating a person with a mental illness and gives the person a right to information and a right to complain to the State Mental Health Authority. The District Child Protection Unit and the Child Welfare Committee are the local authorities for a child kept in an unregistered institution, and Childline on 1098 takes the call.
30-18.caveats: Grade C because the record here is court cases and investigations, not a count of harm across institutions. If a child is already inside such a place, get them out; if they report restraint, beating or sexual abuse, call 112 and 1098, and preserve clothing and medical records. The behavioural alternative is a structured parenting course (item 17) and a child psychiatrist for a genuine disorder. Screen addiction is not a diagnosis in the ICD or the DSM; gaming disorder is, and it is treated as an outpatient problem.

30-19.benefit: A 2015 Cochrane review of 24 school-based trials (5,802 students aged 5 to 18) found that child safety programmes substantially increased self-protective behaviour: in simulated assessments using adult lures, instructed children were 5.7 times more likely to show the protective skills (OR 5.71, 95% CI 1.98-16.51; 795 per 1,000 against 390 per 1,000). Knowledge was still better at six months (SMD 0.69, 95% CI 0.51-0.87), with no increase in fear or anxiety (SMD -0.08, 95% CI -0.22 to 0.07). The UNESCO technical guidance recommends teaching children aged 5 to 8 the anatomical names for genital parts, bodily autonomy and the no-go-tell rule: say no, get away, tell a trusted adult. In India the legal layer is the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, which makes reporting mandatory for anyone who knows of an offence against a child, including a parent, and punishes failure to report; the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 covers a child in need of care and protection. Most children are abused by someone they know, which is why the no-secrets rule matters more than stranger danger.
30-19.caveats: Graded B because the trials measure proxy milestones, protective skills in simulations and questionnaire knowledge, rather than lifetime victimisation. Home rules: teach the anatomical words, say that anyone who asks a child to keep a secret from a parent is breaking a safety rule, and promise the child will not be in trouble for telling. If a child discloses abuse, say it is not their fault, do not bathe them or change their clothes before a forensic examination, and call 112 and 1098; a police complaint can be made at any station whatever the relationship of the person named. Grade C claims about prevalence are not used here for that reason.

30-20.title: Do not let a child ride a motorised two-wheeler before the legal age: a parent who hands over the vehicle is liable, and compensation is cut if the rider was unlicensed
30-20.cost: Free, but you have to arrange the school run: bus, walking group or an adult escort. The hard part is refusing when classmates already ride.
30-20.inPlainWords: India sets no minimum age for riding a bicycle on a public road, and a helmet is the sensible rule from the first ride. Motorised two-wheelers are different: a licence is needed, the minimum age is 16 for a motorcycle with an engine up to 50 cc and 18 for anything larger, and a child below that cannot legally ride one on the road. If a child takes the family scooter and causes a crash, the guardian or owner can be held responsible, the vehicle's registration can be cancelled, and the child's own compensation in a road-accident case is reduced for contributory fault.
30-20.benefit: Under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, as amended in 2019, a person needs a licence to drive a motor vehicle on a public road; the Act allows a licence for a motorcycle of up to 50 cc at 16 and sets 18 for other motor vehicles. Section 199A, inserted by the 2019 amendment, treats the guardian or owner of the vehicle as guilty when a juvenile commits an offence with it and bars that juvenile from holding a learner's licence until 25. Third-party insurance is compulsory, so a crash involving an unlicensed child is handled by the insurer and then reduced for contributory fault. A trauma registry study of 337 children with traffic injuries found traumatic brain injury in 13% of child e-bike riders against 3% of ordinary cyclists, with severe injury odds 2.56 times higher (OR 2.56, 95% CI 1.10-5.88).
30-20.caveats: The age limits are national, while enforcement and helmet rules vary by State. A low-power electric scooter is treated differently from a motorcycle, but the family rule should be the same: no road riding without a licence and a helmet. Never let a child use an adult's phone or account to unlock a shared vehicle. Once a child is old enough, a helmet that fits is not optional (item 21 and chapter 22).
30-20.sources: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. <https://morth.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Zmora O, Peleg K, Klein Y (2019). Pediatric electric bicycle injuries and comparison to other pediatric traffic injuries. Traffic Injury Prevention. <https://doi.org/10.1080/15389588.2019.1608361>

30-16.inPlainWords: Children who are often physically punished show more aggression and psychological problems, feel more distant from parents, and are punished more harshly. Whether spanking makes a child obey on the spot is unclear in the evidence. Adolescents who are often yelled at or called stupid at age 13 show more misconduct and depression the next year, and warm parenting does not cancel that link. In India, hitting a child in school is barred by section 17 of the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, and cruelty to a child is an offence under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, whether the child is at home or in an institution.
30-16.benefit: For physical punishment, one meta-analysis counted only open-hand spanking of the buttocks or limbs. It pooled 75 studies with 111 effect sizes and 160,927 children. Of 17 outcomes, 13 were significantly associated with spanking, all in harmful directions. Cohen's d: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium. Childhood aggression d = 0.37 (95% CI 0.13-0.61). Externalizing problems 0.41 (hitting, rule-breaking). Internalizing 0.24 (anxiety, depression). Mental health problems 0.53. Poor parent-child relationship 0.51. Low self-esteem 0.15. Poor cognitive ability 0.17. Parental physical abuse 0.64. Adult antisocial behaviour 0.36. Adult mental health 0.24. Pooled across 111 effects d = 0.33 (0.29-0.38). Immediate compliance was not clearly linked (d = 0.14, -0.19-0.47), with only 5 effect sizes. Another review of 69 longitudinal studies found spanking reliably predicted later behaviour problems and no long-term benefits; 7 studies counted frequency, 5 found more spanking linked to worse outcomes. For yelling: a study in the United States followed 976 two-parent families. Frequent yelling, cursing, or calling the child stupid or lazy at age 13 predicted more misconduct and depressive symptoms between ages 13 and 14. Parental warmth did not offset the association; the reverse also held, with more misconduct at 13 predicting more yelling later. The Indian legal layer points the same way. Section 17 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 bars physical punishment and mental harassment in school. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 treats assault, abandonment and wilful neglect of a child by a person having care of the child as cruelty and makes it punishable, and it requires anyone who sees such treatment to report it to the police, the Childline service or the Child Welfare Committee. Section 115 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers voluntary hurt, and criminal intimidation is a separate offence.
30-16.caveats: Controversial. These studies are almost all observational, not randomized trials, so causation is unclear. In the spanking meta-analysis, 72% of studies were cross-sectional or relied on recall. A meta-analysis of longitudinal studies found that after adjusting for prior child behaviour, links to externalizing problems fell to 0.07 and internalizing to 0.10; those authors judged the effects small. Another meta-analysis found 'conditional' spanking outperformed 10 of 13 alternative discipline methods for reducing defiance and antisocial behaviour, but severe or predominant spanking did worse than the alternatives. Critics and supporters agree that heavy, frequent hitting and verbal abuse are worse. What to switch to is covered in item 17 of this chapter, and the legal position is settled even where the research is not: a parent who injures a child can be prosecuted for hurt under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and a child in danger can be brought before the Child Welfare Committee under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015. If someone in the household is being beaten, chapter 6 and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 are the route for an adult woman. Anyone may report chronic abuse of a child by calling 112 or 1098; do not force your way into another family's house.
